## Statement

Let $\rho_0,\mu>0$, $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, and $U\in\mathbb R$. Use SI units: length metres, time seconds, velocity $U,A$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, density $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, viscosity $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, diffusivity $\nu$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, periods $L_x,L_y,L_z$ in metres, and $k$ in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. For Cartesian fields use $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_xu_x+\partial_yu_y+\partial_zu_z$ and componentwise $\Delta u$. For $t>0,y>0$ and $x,z\in\mathbb R$, set $I_0=\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}dr$, $E(s)=I_0^{-1}\int_s^\infty e^{-r^2}dr$ for $s\ge0$, and $u(t,x,y,z)=(UE(y/(2\sqrt{\nu t})),0,0)$, with constant pressure. This field is smooth for positive time and positive $y$, solves unsteady Stokes and full constant-density Navier–Stokes because its convective term vanishes, has vector wall trace $(U,0,0)$ for $t>0$, tends to zero as $y\to\infty$, and tends to zero as $t\downarrow0$ for each fixed $y>0$. The corner $(t,y)=(0,0)$ is excluded. For $0<\varepsilon<1$,
$$y\ge2\sqrt{\nu t}\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |u(t,y)|\le\varepsilon|U|.$$

Separately let the domain be the flat three-torus $\mathbb T_{L_x}\times\mathbb T_{L_y}\times\mathbb T_{L_z}$, where $\mathbb T_L=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$ and $L_x,L_y,L_z>0$. Choose an integer $m\ge1$, set $k=2\pi m/L_y$, and take $A\in\mathbb R$. Let $\pi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T_{L_x}\times\mathbb T_{L_y}\times\mathbb T_{L_z}$ be the quotient map. Use the flat metric and tangent-space identification induced by Euclidean translations; equations on the torus mean equations for periodic lifts on $\mathbb R^3$. The periodic lift $\widetilde u(t,x,y,z)=(Ae^{-\nu k^2t}\sin(ky),0,0)$ defines a torus vector field by $u(t,\pi(q))=d\pi_q(\widetilde u(t,q))$; with constant pressure it is a smooth exact Navier–Stokes solution for all $t\in\mathbb R$. Choose $b,c>0$ with $c<L_x/2$, $b<L_y/2$, and $\alpha=kb\in(0,\pi)$. Define the closed lifted loop
$$\widetilde X(t,s)=\left(c\sin(2\pi s)+\frac{A}{\nu k^2}(1-e^{-\nu k^2t})\sin(kb\cos(2\pi s)),\ b\cos(2\pi s),\ 0\right),\quad 0\le s\le1,$$
and put $X(t,s)=\pi(\widetilde X(t,s))$. Its material condition is $\partial_t\widetilde X(t,s)=\widetilde u(t,\widetilde X(t,s))$, and its flat-torus circulation is $\Gamma(t):=\int_0^1\widetilde u(t,\widetilde X(t,s))\cdot\partial_s\widetilde X(t,s)\,ds$. This value is unchanged by translating the lift by a lattice vector in $L_x\mathbb Z\times L_y\mathbb Z\times L_z\mathbb Z$. It has the value $\Gamma(t)=AcC_\alpha e^{-\nu k^2t}$, where $C_\alpha=\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\sin(\alpha\cos\theta)\,d\theta>0$; it is nonconstant if $A\ne0$. These are distinct exact solutions in the selected Newtonian model, not experiments or general boundary-layer claims.

## Statement references

[Mandre, *Fluid Dynamics Lecture Notes*, §3.3.1, Stokes first problem](https://notes.shreyasmandre.com/fluid-dynamics-notes/Ch3.html)

[MIT 2.25 Advanced Fluid Mechanics, *Solution: Stokes First Problem*, all four pages; similarity and wall-stress scaling only](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-25-advanced-fluid-mechanics-fall-2013/6c64b72340cd5b5da9a0d59516b63aec_MIT2_25F13_SolutionStokes1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\rho_0,\mu>0$, $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, wall speed $U$, half-space data, positive-time restriction, torus periods, wave number and loop.

[A1] [[post-fd-continuum-balances]]: continuum balance laws are adopted physical assumptions; these are conditional model deductions.

[A2] [[post-fd-boundary-data]]: wall and initial values are separate inputs; the impulsive corner is outside the smooth claim.

[A3] [[post-fd-newtonian-fourier]]: the selected mechanical closure is Newtonian in the incompressible constant-viscosity branch; heat flux is unused.

[F1] [[def-fd-incompressible-newtonian-model]]: the local equation is $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $\rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u$ for constant $\mu$.

[F2] [[thm-fd-x08]]: the half-space field, Gaussian tail bound, torus shear solution and specified material-loop circulation are as stated, with the corner excluded.

[F3] [[def-fd-x00]] defines Euclidean circulation for a closed piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ as $\int_a^b u(\gamma(s))\cdot\gamma'(s)\,ds$. For the flat quotient, [[thm-fd-x08]] supplies the periodic-lift convention: $X=\pi(\widetilde X)$ is material when $\partial_t\widetilde X=\widetilde u(t,\widetilde X)$, and its circulation is $\int_0^1\widetilde u(t,\widetilde X)\cdot\partial_s\widetilde X\,ds$. Translating the lift by a period-lattice vector changes neither the periodic velocity nor the lift derivative, so the value descends to the specified torus loop.

## Proof

1.1 Set $s=y/(2\sqrt{\nu t})\ge0$. The integral $I_0$ is positive and finite, since its integrand is positive and $e^{-r^2}\le e^{-r}$ for $r\ge1$. Substituting $r=s+z$ in the definition of $E$ and using $(s+z)^2\ge s^2+z^2$ gives $E(s)=I_0^{-1}\int_0^\infty e^{-(s+z)^2}\,dz\le e^{-s^2}I_0^{-1}\int_0^\infty e^{-z^2}\,dz=e^{-s^2}$. If $y\ge2\sqrt{\nu t}\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}$, then $s^2\ge\log(1/\varepsilon)$, so $E(s)\le\varepsilon$ and $|u|\le\varepsilon|U|$. [given, algebra]

1.2 For the periodic lift, div $\widetilde u=0$, $(\widetilde u\cdot\nabla)\widetilde u=0$, and $\partial_t\widetilde u=\nu\Delta\widetilde u$, so the local Newtonian equation holds. Differentiation gives $\partial_t\widetilde X=(Ae^{-\nu k^2t}\sin(kb\cos2\pi s),0,0)=\widetilde u(t,\widetilde X)$, so $X=\pi(\widetilde X)$ is material. By [F3], the circulation is $\int_0^1\widetilde u(t,\widetilde X(t,s))\cdot\partial_s\widetilde X(t,s)\,ds$; parameterize this integral by $\theta=2\pi s$. The base-loop term is $Ac e^{-\nu k^2t}C_\alpha$. The extra term from the moving horizontal shift is proportional to $\int_0^{2\pi}\sin(\alpha\cos\theta)\sin\theta\cos(\alpha\cos\theta)\,d\theta=0$, since its integrand changes sign under $\theta\mapsto2\pi-\theta$. This proves the formula. [A1, A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The first solution is asserted only for $t>0,y>0$; the second circulation is for the specified torus field and loop. They imply no general boundary-layer or Kelvin theorem. [A2, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Example

For the half-space Stokes first-problem model, choose $\nu=1\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $U=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $t=1\,\mathrm s$. At $y=2\sqrt{\log2}\,\mathrm m$, the exact Gaussian-tail estimate gives $|u|\le\tfrac12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For the separate torus shear choose $L_x=L_y=L_z=2\pi\,\mathrm m$, $m=1$, $k=1\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $A=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $b=\pi/3\,\mathrm m$, and $c=1\,\mathrm m$. Then $\alpha=\pi/3$ and
$$\Gamma(t)=2C_{\pi/3}e^{-t/(1\,\mathrm s)}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}},\qquad C_{\pi/3}=\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\sin((\pi/3)\cos\theta)\,d\theta>0.$$
These are exact model values, not measured velocity or circulation.

[Mandre, *Fluid Dynamics Lecture Notes*, §3.3.1](https://notes.shreyasmandre.com/fluid-dynamics-notes/Ch3.html)

**Given:** The positive-time half-space and torus solutions, parameters above, and specified loop.

[F1] [[pthm-fd-px08-prediction]]: the half-space field obeys $|u|\le|U|e^{-y^2/(4\nu t)}$, and the torus material-loop circulation is $AcC_\alpha e^{-\nu k^2t}$.

[F2] [[def-fd-x00]] defines Euclidean circulation for closed piecewise-$C^1$ curves as $\int u(\gamma(s))\cdot\gamma'(s)\,ds$. For the torus loop, the physical supplier [F1] instead specifies the flat-quotient lift $X=\pi(\widetilde X)$, the periodic velocity $\widetilde u$, and the circulation $\int_0^1\widetilde u(t,\widetilde X(t,s))\cdot\partial_s\widetilde X(t,s)\,ds$. The given lift is closed, and period-lattice translations preserve this integral; this is the convention used for the torus value below.

## Proof

1.1 At the selected height $y^2/(4\nu t)=\log2$, so $|u|\le1\cdot e^{-\log2}=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Interpret the torus circulation as the periodic-lift integral in [F2], whose value is supplied by [F1]. For the torus parameters, $\nu k^2=1\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $Ac=2\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and $\alpha=kb=\pi/3$; substitution gives the displayed circulation. Positivity of $C_{\pi/3}$ follows from the theorem's stated range. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Both outputs are deductions for their specified exact solutions and make no general empirical or boundary-layer claim. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
